# Assinafy API and SDK reference

This reference combines the checked-in official production OpenAPI snapshot with the SDK's public resource methods. The OpenAPI snapshot is the canonical full HTTP payload contract; source XML comments document .NET parameters and behavior.

The checked-in production snapshot uses low-entropy `example-*` credential and token placeholders and RFC-reserved `example.com` email addresses. Its API structure and schemas match the production contract.

- Source: https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json
- Snapshot SHA-256: `eb47cf0dee3bd9c259f5b50c65ee4176b9a36ab1342dc92189f771f1688b52a5`
- OpenAPI: `3.1.0`; API info version: `1.0.0`
- API surface: 147 documented production operations across 112 paths, 62 component schemas, and 31 webhook event payloads.

The API wraps JSON successes and errors as `{"status": number, "message": string|null, "data": ...}`. Binary routes return raw bytes. Authenticated routes accept a bearer token or `X-Api-Key`; signer routes use the `signer-access-code` query parameter; public routes deliberately receive no configured SDK credential.

Every request must use HTTPS with TLS 1.2 or higher. TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are rejected during the handshake, so they fail as a connection error (`NetworkException`), never as an HTTP status.

Requests are rate-limited per minute: per user when authenticated, per IP address otherwise, with tighter limits on a few sensitive routes (payments, coupons, MFA, OAuth). Limited responses carry `X-Rate-Limit-Limit`, `X-Rate-Limit-Remaining`, and `X-Rate-Limit-Reset` (seconds until the window resets); past the limit the API answers `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` (seconds). The SDK does not retry; `ApiException` exposes `RateLimitLimit`, `RateLimitRemaining`, `RateLimitReset`, and `RetryAfter`.

The four OAuth routes are the deliberate exception to the envelope: they implement the RFC 6749 §5.1/§5.2, OpenID Connect §5.3.2, and RFC 9728 body contracts as flat JSON objects, because no standard OAuth client library would look for `access_token` or `error` nested inside a `data` key. `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` is additionally served at the API host root, outside the `/v1` base path, per RFC 8615.

## Official integration guidance

### Quick Start

Steps to quickly start using the API. By the end you'll be able to create a document and invite signers.

### 1. Create a user account

During development, create a user account in the **sandbox** (https://app-sandbox.assinafy.com.br). For integrations using an API key, create a *separate* user account (e.g. *My App*) so you can grant it only the access it needs. Use the production app (https://app.assinafy.com.br) once you go live.

### 2. Set up credentials

Generate an **API key** from the *My Account → API* page in the Assinafy app, and note your **workspace account ID** from *My Account → Workspaces*. Use the API key only from a back-end system — never store it in client-side code.

For sandbox plan/credit purchases, use the test card `5510 3647 0363 3414`.

### 3. Upload a document

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/{account_id}/documents" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -F 'file=@/tmp/document.pdf'
```

Save the returned document `id` for the next steps.

### 4. Create signers

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/{account_id}/signers" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "full_name": "John Dove", "email": "john@example.com" }'
```

Save each signer `id`.

### 5. Request signatures

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/documents/{document_id}/assignments" \
  -H 'X-Api-Key: {api_key}' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{ "method": "virtual", "signers": [{ "id": "{signer_id}" }] }'
```

The `virtual` method requires no input from the signer. To collect input fields, use the `collect` method — see the Assignment section.

### SDKs & Tools

Official client libraries, a command-line tool, an MCP server and an n8n node — all built against the same OpenAPI document that generates this reference. Source for everything lives at [github.com/assinafy](https://github.com/assinafy).

Every SDK exposes the same operations and reads the same credentials:

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `ASSINAFY_API_KEY` | API key, sent as the `X-Api-Key` header. Create it from *My Account → API*. |
| `ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID` | Workspace account id, from *My Account → Workspaces*. |
| `ASSINAFY_BASE_URL` | `https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1` while developing, `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1` in production. |

An API key is a long-lived secret with full workspace access. Use it only from a back-end system — never in a browser bundle or a shipped mobile app.

### Which Java package?

Two Java artifacts exist and they are close to identical — both ship `com.assinafy.sdk.AssinafyClient` covering the same operations. Use **java-sdk** (`com.assinafy:assinafy-sdk`) for new integrations. **webforms-java-client** (`com.assinafy:webforms-java-client-sdk`, [source](https://github.com/assinafy/webforms-java-client)) is the same client with an older setter-style options builder, kept for integrations already on it; despite the name it carries no webforms-specific API.

Neither is published to Maven Central. Both resolve from GitHub Packages at `https://maven.pkg.github.com/assinafy/{repository}`, which requires a GitHub personal access token with `read:packages` even for public artifacts.

### Which TypeScript package?

`@assinafy/sdk` is the general-purpose REST client and the right default. [`@assinafy/chat-sdk`](https://github.com/assinafy/chat-sdk) bundles that same client *plus* chat orchestration, renderable cards, adapter and state contracts, and provider-neutral AI tool definitions — reach for it only when you are building a conversational signing experience.

## Mobile SDKs

| Platform | Install | Source |
|----------|---------|--------|
| iOS / macOS | SwiftPM — add the package URL `https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-ios-sdk.git` and pin *Up to Next Major* from the current release | [mobile-ios-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-ios-sdk) |
| Android | Gradle — `implementation("com.assinafy:assinafy-android-sdk:{version}")`, resolved from GitHub Packages (token required) | [mobile-android-sdk](https://github.com/assinafy/mobile-android-sdk) |

Both are released on GitHub Releases; take the current version from the *Releases* page of the repository rather than a number quoted here.

**Never embed an account API key in a distributed app.** A key extracted from an app bundle grants full access to the workspace. Have the app authenticate against your own back end and receive a short-lived access token, or keep account operations server-side entirely.

## Command line

[`@assinafy/cli`](https://github.com/assinafy/assinafy-cli) exposes the API as a terminal tool: readable tables by default, `--json` for scripting, and named profiles so sandbox and production credentials stay apart.

```shell
npm install -g @assinafy/cli
assinafy login
assinafy send contract.pdf --signer "Ana Lima <ana@example.com>" --message "Please sign this contract"
```

## MCP server

A Model Context Protocol server that lets an AI assistant work with documents in your workspace. It is **hosted by Assinafy — there is nothing to install or deploy**.

| | |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | `POST https://mcp.assinafy.com.br/mcp` |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP (remote) |
| Authentication | OAuth 2.0 only — API keys are not accepted |

Add it to your MCP client as a **remote HTTP** server; there is no local command to run. On first use the client opens a browser window where you sign in to Assinafy, choose a workspace and approve the requested permissions. You do not create an OAuth application or enter a client ID, client secret, API key or workspace header — the client identifies itself with a Client ID Metadata Document. For example, in Claude Code:

```shell
claude mcp add --transport http assinafy https://mcp.assinafy.com.br/mcp
claude mcp login assinafy
```

The default scopes requested are `account:read`, `documents:read`, `documents:write`, `templates:read` and `templates:write`, plus `offline_access` when the client wants a refresh token. Setup for other clients (VS Code, Codex and more) is in the [MCP server documentation](https://github.com/assinafy/mcp-server/blob/main/README.en.md).

Eleven tools are exposed:

- **Documents** — `assinafy_find_documents`, `assinafy_prepare_document`, `assinafy_download_document`, `assinafy_verify_document`, `assinafy_delete_document`
- **Signature requests** — `assinafy_request_signatures`, `assinafy_follow_up_assignment`, `assinafy_check_fields`
- **Signers** — `assinafy_find_signers`, `assinafy_save_signer`
- **Templates** — `assinafy_find_templates`

Template creation, page-layout editing, role configuration and signer-side operations (signing, verification codes, term acceptance) are deliberately not exposed to assistants. Use the REST API for those.

## n8n

[`@assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy`](https://github.com/assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy) ships three pieces: an **Assinafy** action node covering assignments, documents, fields, signers, tags, templates, webhooks and workspaces; an **Assinafy Trigger** webhook node; and a shared **Assinafy API** credential holding the API key, the account id and the environment (production, sandbox or a custom base URL).

On self-hosted n8n, open **Settings → Community Nodes** and enter `@assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy`, or install it in the n8n container directly:

```shell
npm install @assinafy/n8n-nodes-assinafy
```

The Trigger node derives its webhook URL authentication from the credential and can additionally verify an HMAC-SHA256 payload signature, so a subscription created from n8n needs no extra webhook setup on the Assinafy side. Availability in n8n Cloud follows n8n's own community-node review.

## In practice

```javascript
import { AssinafyClient } from '@assinafy/sdk';

const client = new AssinafyClient({
  apiKey: process.env.ASSINAFY_API_KEY,
  accountId: process.env.ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID,
});

const result = await client.uploadAndRequestSignatures({
  source: { filePath: './contract.pdf' },
  signers: [{ name: 'John Dove', email: 'john@example.com' }],
  message: 'Please sign this contract',
});

console.log(result.document.id);
```

```python
import os
from assinafy import AssinafyClient

with AssinafyClient(
    api_key=os.environ['ASSINAFY_API_KEY'],
    account_id=os.environ['ASSINAFY_ACCOUNT_ID'],
) as client:
    result = client.upload_and_request_signatures(
        source={'file_path': './contract.pdf'},
        signers=[{'full_name': 'John Dove', 'email': 'john@example.com'}],
        message='Please sign this contract',
    )
    print(result['document']['id'])
```

### OpenAPI & API Clients

This reference is generated from a single OpenAPI 3.0 document. You can download that document and load it into any OpenAPI-aware tool — Postman, Insomnia, a code generator, or your editor.

## Download the spec

The document is served at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json` and always describes what is currently deployed:

```shell
curl -o assinafy-openapi.json "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json"
```


## Postman

There are two ways in.

**Fork the ready-made collection.** Open the [Assinafy API workspace on Postman](https://www.postman.com/assinafy/assinafy-api/overview), select the collection, then **Fork** it into your own workspace.

**Or import the spec yourself:**

1. **Import → Link**, paste `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json` and confirm. Postman creates a request for every operation, grouped by section.
2. On the new collection, open **Authorization**, choose **API Key**, set *Key* to `X-Api-Key`, *Value* to `{{api_key}}` and *Add to* **Header**. Every request inherits it.
3. Create an **environment** holding `base_url` (`https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1` while developing) and `api_key`. Keep the key in the environment rather than the collection so it does not travel with an exported or shared collection.

## Insomnia

1. **Create → Import → From URL**, paste `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json`.
2. Open **Manage Environments** on the imported collection and add:

```json
{
  "base_url": "https://sandbox.assinafy.com.br/v1",
  "api_key": "your-api-key"
}
```

3. On the collection's **Headers** tab add `X-Api-Key` with value `{{ _.api_key }}` so every request inherits it.

Switching between sandbox and production is then a matter of selecting a different environment.

## Generate your own client

The document works with the usual generators:

```shell
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate \
  -i https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/docs/openapi.json \
  -g python \
  -o ./assinafy-client
```

Worth weighing first: the official SDKs listed under *SDKs & Tools* already unwrap the `{ status, message, data }` envelope, surface the `X-Pagination-*` response headers as pagination objects, and handle multipart document upload. A generated client hands you the raw envelope on every call and leaves that work to you.

### Authentication

Authentication can be done in three ways:

- API key in the `X-Api-Key` header: `X-Api-Key: {api-key}`
- Access token in the `Authorization` header: `Authorization: Bearer {access-token}`
- Access token as a URL parameter: `?access-token={access-token}`

The **recommended** method is an API key, which you create from the settings page in the Assinafy app. An access token is obtained through login with email and password; it is a JWT that usually expires in one hour.

Building an application that **other people** connect to their own workspace? Don't ask for their API key: use OAuth, which gives your app a token limited to what the user approved. See **OAuth Integration Guide**.

### OAuth Integration Guide

Build an application that **other people connect to their own Assinafy workspace**, without ever handling their password or API key. The user approves your app once; you receive tokens limited to the permissions they approved and to one workspace. Standard OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect libraries work unchanged.

### Do you need OAuth?

| | API key | OAuth |
|---|---|---|
| Acts on | **Your own** workspace | **Someone else's** workspace, with their permission |
| Can do | Everything your account can do | Only what the user approved |
| The user can switch it off | No | Yes, at any time |
| Choose it when | You automate your own account | You build an app that other people connect |

Automating your own workspace? Keep using your API key; nothing in this guide applies.

### How it works

1. Your app sends the user's browser to the authorization server, `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`.
2. The user signs in, picks **one** workspace and approves your app.
3. The browser comes back to your site with a one-time code.
4. Your server exchanges the code for tokens at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token`.
5. Your server calls this API with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`.

Two hosts on purpose: the browser page lives on the authorization server, and everything your code calls lives on this API.

### Create your application

You must be an **owner** of the workspace that will own the application, and the workspace's plan must include OAuth applications. In the Assinafy app (https://app.assinafy.com.br), open **Settings → OAuth applications → New application**.

| Field | What to put |
|---|---|
| Name | What users see on the approval screen |
| Description | One sentence on what the app does with their documents |
| Logo URL | Optional, an `https://` image |
| Redirect URIs | Where users return after approving, e.g. `https://myapp.com/oauth/callback`. Must be `https://`, without `#`, and is matched **exactly**: `…/callback` and `…/callback/` are different. Add one per environment you run. For local development use an https tunnel; `http://localhost` is not accepted |
| Permissions | The **most** your app will ever request. You can ask for less at connect time, never more |
| Type | **Confidential** if your code runs on a server you control; **Public** if it runs on the user's device and cannot keep a secret. Cannot be changed later |

You get a `client_id` (public) and, for Confidential apps, a `client_secret`.

> **The secret is shown once.** Store it in your server's secret storage straight away. If it is lost, rotate it: the old secret stops working immediately, so deploy the new one at once. Deleting the application disconnects every user immediately.

Building one product that **many different Assinafy customers** will connect? Talk to us first: we can register it as a verified application owned by no single workspace, with one `client_id` for every customer.

### Discovery

Most OAuth libraries only need the issuer, `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`, and read the rest from its metadata document. If you configure URLs by hand, copy them from there:

```shell
curl "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server"
```

```json
{
  "issuer": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br",
  "authorization_endpoint": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/oauth/authorize",
  "token_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token",
  "revocation_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/revoke",
  "userinfo_endpoint": "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/userinfo",
  "jwks_uri": "https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/jwks.json",
  "response_types_supported": ["code"],
  "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"],
  "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["client_secret_post", "none"]
}
```

The metadata and key documents are served **only** by the authorization server. This API serves its own protected-resource metadata at `https://api.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.

### Connect a user

#### 1. Create a PKCE pair and a state

PKCE is required for **every** application, Confidential ones included. Create a new pair for each connection attempt:

```js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';

const b64url = (buf) => buf.toString('base64url');

const codeVerifier  = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(32));
const codeChallenge = b64url(crypto.createHash('sha256').update(codeVerifier).digest());
const state         = b64url(crypto.randomBytes(16));

// Keep codeVerifier and state in the user's session: step 3 and 4 need them.
```

The verifier must be 43 to 128 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~`.

#### 2. Send the browser to the authorization server

Use a full page navigation (a link or a redirect), not an AJAX call. Shown unencoded for readability; URL-encode every value:

```
https://auth.assinafy.com.br/oauth/authorize
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
  &redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/oauth/callback
  &scope=documents:read documents:write offline_access
  &state=STATE
  &code_challenge=CODE_CHALLENGE
  &code_challenge_method=S256
  &resource=https://api.assinafy.com.br
```

| Parameter | Notes |
|---|---|
| `redirect_uri` | One of your registered URIs, character for character |
| `scope` | Space-separated, within what the application is registered for |
| `state` | Random per attempt; your CSRF protection |
| `code_challenge_method` | Only `S256` |
| `resource` | `https://api.assinafy.com.br`, naming the API the token is for. Recommended |
| `nonce` | Optional, echoed in the `id_token` when you request `openid` |

If the `client_id` or `redirect_uri` is wrong, the user is **not** sent back to you: the authorization server shows an error on its own page, because redirecting to an unverified address would be unsafe. Users reporting that they are stuck on an Assinafy error page usually means one of those two values is wrong.

#### 3. Handle the return

Approved:

```
https://myapp.com/oauth/callback?code=…&state=…&iss=https://auth.assinafy.com.br
```

Declined or invalid:

```
https://myapp.com/oauth/callback?error=access_denied&error_description=…&state=…&iss=https://auth.assinafy.com.br
```

Before anything else, check that `state` equals what you stored and that `iss` equals `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`. If either differs, stop: the response is not yours.

#### 4. Exchange the code for tokens

From your server. The code is single-use and expires **60 seconds** after approval.

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  -d grant_type=authorization_code \
  -d code=THE_CODE \
  -d redirect_uri=https://myapp.com/oauth/callback \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d code_verifier=THE_CODE_VERIFIER \
  -d resource=https://api.assinafy.com.br
```

Public applications send the same request without `client_secret`.

```json
{
  "access_token": "…",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "scope": "documents:read documents:write",
  "refresh_token": "…",
  "id_token": "…"
}
```

- `refresh_token` is present only when you requested `offline_access`; `id_token` only when you requested `openid`. `offline_access` itself never appears in `scope`: it only asks for a refresh token and isn't a permission the access token carries.
- `scope` is what you **actually** received. Read it instead of assuming.
- OAuth token responses are plain JSON objects, not wrapped in the `{ status, message, data }` envelope the rest of this API uses.

#### 5. Find the workspace, then call the API

A token belongs to the one workspace the user picked. With an OAuth token, the workspace list returns exactly that workspace:

```shell
curl "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts" \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN'
```

Store `data[0].id` next to the tokens, then call the API:

```shell
curl "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/WORKSPACE_ID/documents" \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN'
```

Always send the token in the `Authorization: Bearer` header. A token sent as `X-Api-Key` or in the query string is refused.

### Permissions (scopes)

| Scope | Lets your app |
|---|---|
| `documents:read` | Read documents, their signers, assignments and activity, the WhatsApp notifications sent for an assignment, and webhook event types and delivery history |
| `documents:write` | Create documents and send them for signature |
| `templates:read` | Read templates |
| `templates:write` | Create and change templates |
| `account:read` | Read the workspace's profile, theme and logo, its document KPIs (stats), its webhook subscription and endpoints, and which signing features it can use |
| `webhooks:write` | Change where and which webhook events are delivered, deactivate the webhook subscription, manage webhook endpoints, get a new signing secret for one (by turning signing on or rotating it), and re-send a delivery (**Retry Webhook Dispatch**) |
| `openid` | Receive an `id_token` identifying the user |
| `profile` | Read the user's name |
| `email` | Read the user's email and whether it is verified |
| `offline_access` | Receive a refresh token, to keep working while the user is away |

- Request the minimum. Every permission is another line the user reads before deciding.
- `documents:write` can spend the workspace's notification credits, since sending for signature notifies signers.
- The user approves everything you requested, or nothing. If a feature needs more later, run the flow again requesting the larger set.
- Billing and subscriptions, workspace membership, credentials and administration are **never** available to an OAuth token, whatever its scopes.

Calling an endpoint without the scope it requires returns `403` with a challenge naming the missing scope:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="documents:write", resource_metadata="https://api.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
```

Treat it as a prompt to reconnect with that scope added, not as a request to retry. A `403` without this header has another cause: a different workspace, the user's own role, or an area OAuth tokens can never reach.

### Resource indicators

`resource` (RFC 8707) names **which service** a token is for. Omit it and you get a token for
this API — that is what every direct integration wants, and nothing about it has changed.

Assinafy also runs a separate MCP server, which is its own protected resource. A token minted
for it authenticates against *that* server and is refused here, and the reverse is also true.
If you are calling this API directly, send `https://api.assinafy.com.br` or omit the parameter.

A refresh may repeat the original `resource` but never change it; a different value is
rejected with `invalid_target`.

> **Operator note.** The confidential client backing Assinafy's own MCP server is an
> **internal-service client** (`is_internal_service`), provisioned outside this
> self-serve flow. It has no `redirect_uris` and cannot pass through the ordinary
> secret-rotation endpoint — that write requires `redirect_uris` under the client's
> default validation scenario, which an internal-service client deliberately has none
> of. If its secret leaks, the recovery path is **disable the client and provision a
> new one**, then reconfigure the MCP server with the new credentials — not "rotate the
> secret."

### One connection, one workspace

The integration mistake we see most often. A token works only for the workspace the user chose; calling any other workspace returns `403`, even one the same user belongs to. If your customer uses several workspaces, connect each one separately and keep tokens per workspace.

### Refresh tokens

Access tokens last **1 hour**. With `offline_access`, renew them without the user:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/token" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  -d grant_type=refresh_token \
  -d refresh_token=CURRENT_REFRESH_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

Every refresh returns a **new** refresh token and retires the old one.

> **Using an old refresh token disconnects the user.** A reused refresh token cannot be told apart from a stolen one being replayed, so it ends the whole connection: every token stops working and the user must connect again.
>
> 1. Save the new refresh token before doing anything else with the response.
> 2. Treat a timeout as "maybe it worked": re-read your saved token before retrying, never retry blindly with the old one.
> 3. Refresh one at a time per connection.

- A refresh token is valid for **30 days**, and every refresh returns a new one with a fresh 30 days. A connection only expires if your app goes 30 days without refreshing; after that, the user has to reconnect.
- If the user approves your app again with different permissions, the previous tokens stop working immediately.

### Disconnecting

When a user disconnects in your product, revoke the token instead of only deleting it. The endpoint always answers `200`:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/revoke" \
  -d token=THE_REFRESH_OR_ACCESS_TOKEN \
  -d client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID \
  -d client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
```

Users can also revoke your app themselves under **Connected apps** in their Assinafy profile. Deleting or disabling your application has the same effect. In every case your tokens stop working at once: handle the `401` by asking the user to connect again.

> **Revoking a token requires the `client_id` that owns it.** `/oauth/revoke` only revokes a token issued to the client authenticating the call. This matters for an RFC 8693 exchanged token specifically: it carries the *original* (front-end resource) client's id, not the service client that exchanged it — so a back-channel service client can never revoke a token it derived, and the call still answers `200` per RFC 7009's always-succeed contract, giving no indication that nothing happened. That derived token is inherently short-lived (bounded by the exchanged-token TTL), so it ages out on its own; do not build a cleanup call expecting revoke to work on it.

### Verification and limits

- New applications are **unverified**: the approval screen warns that Assinafy has not reviewed the app, and it can be connected to at most **25 workspaces**. Before launching beyond a pilot, ask us to verify it, telling us what the app does and why it needs each permission.
- The authorize and token endpoints accept **50 requests per minute per IP**. Normal traffic stays far below that; hitting it usually means a refresh loop.
- Applications are created in the Assinafy app, not through an API.

### Errors

On your redirect URI (`?error=…`):

| `error` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `access_denied` | The user declined |
| `invalid_scope` | A scope your application is not registered for, or none |
| `invalid_request` | Missing or malformed PKCE parameters |
| `unsupported_response_type` | Anything other than `response_type=code` |
| `invalid_target` | A `resource` other than `https://api.assinafy.com.br` |

From the token endpoint (`{ "error": "…", "error_description": "…" }`):

| `error` | Usual causes |
|---|---|
| `invalid_grant` | Code expired or already used, wrong `code_verifier` or `redirect_uri`; refresh token already used or expired, or the user reconnected with different permissions |
| `invalid_client` | Wrong `client_id` or secret, or the application is disabled |
| `invalid_target` | `resource` does not match what was authorized |
| `unsupported_grant_type` | Only `authorization_code` and `refresh_token` exist |

From API calls:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `401` | Token expired, revoked, or not sent as `Bearer`. Refresh; if that fails, ask the user to reconnect |
| `403` with `insufficient_scope` | Missing permission. Reconnect requesting the scope in `WWW-Authenticate` |
| `403` otherwise | Another workspace, or an area OAuth tokens cannot reach |
| `429` | Too many requests. Back off and retry later |

### Signing users in (OpenID Connect)

Request `openid`, plus `profile` and/or `email`, to receive an `id_token`: a signed JWT saying who approved. Validate it with any OpenID Connect library:

- signature `RS256`, keys at `https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/jwks.json` (match the `kid`);
- `iss` equals `https://auth.assinafy.com.br`;
- `aud` equals your `client_id`;
- `exp` is in the future, and `nonce` matches the one you sent, if any.

`sub` is the user's stable identifier. For their name and email, call **OpenID Connect userinfo** (`GET https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/oauth/userinfo`).

### AI assistants

Claude, Claude Code and ChatGPT connect to Assinafy on their own through their connector settings. Your users do not need you to build or register anything for them.

### Before you go live

- A new PKCE verifier and `state` for every connection attempt
- `state` and `iss` checked on your redirect URI
- `client_secret` only on your server, never in a mobile app, browser code or a repository
- The new refresh token saved before use, and one refresh at a time per connection
- `401` handled: refresh, and if that fails, ask the user to reconnect
- The workspace id stored per connection, and the returned `scope` read
- Every production redirect URI registered, `https://` and exact
- Only the permissions you need
- Tokens revoked when a user disconnects
- Verification requested


### Embedded Signing Guide

## Embedded signing

Show Assinafy's signing screen **inside your own app**, in an iframe, so your signers never leave your product. Your backend asks Assinafy for a short-lived signing URL, your page loads it in an iframe, and the frame tells your page when the signer is done.

### Before you start

- Your plan must include the **Embed** feature. Without it the calls below answer `403` with code `PlanRestricted`. Contact sales or your account manager to have it enabled.
- Minting sessions needs an **API key** (or a user bearer token). Tokens issued to an OAuth application cannot mint embed sessions.
- Everything that creates sessions runs on **your backend**. Never ship your API key to the browser.

### 1. Register the origins that may embed

Assinafy only renders the signing screen inside pages whose origin you have registered. Add each origin with `POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/embed-origins`:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/accounts/{accountId}/embed-origins" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: {api-key}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"origin": "https://app.example.com"}'
```

- List them with `GET`, change one with `PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/embed-origins/{originId}` and remove one with `DELETE` on the same path.
- Each origin is an exact `https://host[:port]`, with no path, query, fragment or wildcard. `http` is accepted only for `localhost` and `127.0.0.1`.
- Up to 10 origins per account.
- With no origins, embedding is disabled: new sessions are refused until you register one again.

### 2. Create embedded signers

When you create the assignment, mark each signer that will sign inside your app with `"embedded": true`:

```json
{
  "method": "virtual",
  "signers": [
    {
      "id": "5f2c1d9e8a7b6c5d4e3f2a1b",
      "verification_method": "Email",
      "notification_methods": ["Email"],
      "embedded": true
    }
  ]
}
```

- Embedded signers use the `Email` or `Whatsapp` verification method.
- In the assignment's `signing_urls`, your backend gets no link for an embedded signer. Their entry looks like this:

```json
{ "signer_id": "5f2c1d9e8a7b6c5d4e3f2a1b", "url": null, "embedded": true }
```

- Embedded signers still receive the normal invitation, which carries the 6-digit code they type in the frame. The invitation also works on its own: a signer can finish from it outside your app, and an open frame then posts `signed` with `via: "external"`.
- Need the signer to sign **only** inside your app, with no invitation at all? Talk to your account manager: it takes a setup we enable per account.

### 3. Mint a session each time you show the frame

When the signer reaches the signing step in your app, your backend calls:

```shell
curl -X POST "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/documents/{documentId}/assignments/{assignmentId}/signers/{signerId}/embed-sessions" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: {api-key}"
```

```json
{
  "url": "https://app.assinafy.com.br/embed/3b1f0c7e9a2d4c58b6e1f4a07d93c2e85a1b0f6d4c7e2a9183b5d6f0e4c8a712",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-04T12:05:00Z"
}
```

- The URL is valid for **5 minutes** and works **once**. Mint a new one every time you display the iframe (including reloads); never store or reuse it.
- Rate limit: 30 sessions per signer per hour.
- The sandbox environment uses `https://app-sandbox.assinafy.com.br` as the iframe origin.
- A signer of an envelope: mint the session on any of their documents of it still waiting for them. The frame lists every document still in the envelope they have to sign, and the code their envelope invitation carries verifies them there, as does the code a reminder of the envelope or of that document sends.

Refusals:

| Status | Code | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `400` | `embed_not_enabled_for_signer` | The signer was not marked `embedded` on the assignment |
| `403` | `PlanRestricted` | The account's plan does not include `Embed` |
| `404` | | The document, assignment or signer was not found in your account, or the signer is not on that assignment |
| `409` | `already_signed` | The signer already signed |
| `409` | `document_not_ready` | The assignment was created while the document was still being uploaded or processed. **Retry**: mint again in a few seconds |
| `409` | `document_unavailable` | The document can no longer be signed (cancelled, declined, expired or finished), or the signer's step is not active yet (sequential signing) |
| `409` | `embed_origins_missing` | No embed origins are registered |
| `429` | | Too many sessions minted for this signer |

This only happens when you create the assignment right after uploading, before Assinafy has finished preparing the file: retry the mint after a few seconds. Once the assignment exists on a prepared document (including documents created from a template), the document is already signable. Don't treat the `document_metadata_ready` webhook as a signal to mint: it can fire before the assignment exists, and minting without an assignment returns `404`.

### 4. Load the iframe and listen to it

The frame and your page talk through `postMessage`. Every message is `{ "v": 1, "type": "assinafy:<event>", "payload": ... }`.

The handshake:

1. Your page sends `{ v: 1, type: "assinafy:hello" }` to the frame, starting on the iframe's `load` event and repeating it every 500 ms until the frame answers `ready` or `error` (for up to 10 seconds). Repeating makes the order irrelevant: either side can be first. This is the only message your page ever sends.
2. The frame checks that it is embedded by one of your registered origins. A `hello` from an origin that is not registered gets `error` with `origin_not_allowed` right away; if no `hello` arrives within 10 seconds, the frame posts the same error. Either way it shows "embedding not allowed here", without any document data.
3. It then posts `ready`, and from then on replies to your origin only.

If the frame reloads (the signer refreshes it, for example), it runs the handshake again: the snippet below says hello on every `load`, and the frame posts `ready` again. Handle `ready` more than once.

Accept messages **only** from the Assinafy origin **and** from your own iframe window. Checking both matters: the origin alone does not prove the message came from your frame.

```html
<iframe id="sign" allow="clipboard-write; fullscreen" style="width:100%;height:600px;border:0"></iframe>
<script>
  // The origin that serves the signing screen (sandbox: https://app-sandbox.assinafy.com.br).
  var ASSINAFY_ORIGIN = "https://app.assinafy.com.br";

  function openSigning(sessionUrl, handlers) {
    var iframe = document.getElementById("sign");
    var helloTimer = null;

    function stopHello() {
      if (helloTimer) {
        clearInterval(helloTimer);
        helloTimer = null;
      }
    }

    // Say hello until the frame answers: every 500 ms, for up to 10 s.
    function startHello() {
      var tries = 0;
      stopHello();
      function hello() {
        iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ v: 1, type: "assinafy:hello" }, ASSINAFY_ORIGIN);
        tries += 1;
        if (tries >= 20) stopHello();
      }
      hello();
      helloTimer = setInterval(hello, 500);
    }

    function onMessage(event) {
      if (event.origin !== ASSINAFY_ORIGIN) return;
      if (event.source !== iframe.contentWindow) return;

      var msg = event.data;
      if (!msg || msg.v !== 1 || typeof msg.type !== "string") return;
      if (msg.type.indexOf("assinafy:") !== 0) return;

      var name = msg.type.slice("assinafy:".length);
      if (name === "ready" || name === "error") stopHello();
      if (name === "resize" && msg.payload && typeof msg.payload.height === "number") {
        iframe.style.height = Math.max(msg.payload.height, 200) + "px";
      }
      if (handlers && handlers[name]) {
        handlers[name](msg.payload);
      }
    }

    window.addEventListener("message", onMessage);
    iframe.addEventListener("load", startHello);
    iframe.src = sessionUrl; // a freshly minted URL from your backend

    return function close() {
      stopHello();
      window.removeEventListener("message", onMessage);
      iframe.removeEventListener("load", startHello);
      iframe.src = "about:blank";
    };
  }

  // Usage: fetch a new session URL from YOUR backend, then
  // openSigning(url, {
  //   signed: function (p) { /* show a success state; may be called twice */ },
  //   error: function (p) { console.warn(p.code, p.message); }
  // });
</script>
```

The iframe starts at 600 px high; the frame then reports its height with `resize` and the snippet follows it.

#### Events from the frame

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `ready` | `{document_id, signer_id}` | The handshake passed: the frame verified your origin and now shows the code screen or the signing screen. Posted again after the frame reloads |
| `signed` | `{document_id, signer_id, via}` | The signer completed. `via` is `"embed"` when they signed in the frame or `"external"` when they finished elsewhere, for example from the invitation |
| `declined` | `{document_id, signer_id, via}` | The signer declined, or the document was declined by someone else |
| `resize` | `{height}` | The content height changed |
| `error` | `{code, message}` | See the codes below |

Error codes:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `origin_not_allowed` | The embedding page's origin is not registered |
| `session_expired` | The URL expired or was already used, or the signer's access code changed because you edited their e-mail or phone. Mint a new session |
| `not_embedded` | The signer is not marked `embedded` |
| `document_unavailable` | The document was cancelled, declined or expired, or is not ready for signing yet |
| `already_signed` | The signer already signed |
| `access_closed` | The signer's access is closed |

Good to know:

- `session_expired`, `already_signed`, `document_unavailable`, `not_embedded` and `origin_not_allowed` can arrive **before** the handshake. The frame has not verified your origin yet, so it posts them to any parent (`"*"`) and they carry only `code` and `message`, never document data. Your origin and source checks still apply to them.
- `signed` and `declined` are terminal, but may be delivered **more than once** (for example after the frame reloads on the done screen). Handle them idempotently.

### Code delivery and resending

The 6-digit code arrives in the invitation, not in the frame, and the frame has no resend button. To send it again, call the regular account-side endpoint from your backend (the same code is resent, so a frame that is already open keeps working):

```shell
curl -X PUT "https://api.assinafy.com.br/v1/documents/{documentId}/assignments/{assignmentId}/signers/{signerId}/resend" \
  -H "X-Api-Key: {api-key}"
```

For a signer of an envelope, resend for the document the session was minted on, or remind them of the whole envelope (`PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/signers/{signerId}/resend`), whose code verifies them in the frame of any of their documents.

Editing the signer's e-mail or phone (`PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/signers/{signerId}`) before they verify issues them a new code and a new access code: an open frame then posts `error` with `session_expired`, and you mint a new session.

### Webhooks are the source of truth

Frame events are UI hints: the signer can close the tab, lose connection or finish from the invitation, and a hostile page could try to forge a message. Treat `signed` only as a cue to refresh your screen, and confirm the outcome from the webhooks (see **Webhook Payloads**), or by reading the document, before you unlock anything on your side.


### Accounts

Workspace accounts: profile, logo and theme.

### Signers

Manage the signing parties of a workspace.

### Documents

Create, list, download, tag and delete documents.

### Envelopes

Send several documents to the same signers at once. Each document keeps its own assignment, status, certificate, downloads and webhooks; the envelope groups them.

### Availability

Creating an envelope needs the Envelopes feature on the workspace's plan (added to every plan, contract and subscription when it arrived): without it, `POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes` answers `403` with code `PlanRestricted`. Adding a document to an envelope and estimating an envelope's cost need it too; every other envelope route works for every workspace. OAuth apps create, change, cancel and delete with `documents:write` and read with `documents:read`.

### Creating

`POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes` takes up to 20 documents, each uploaded and processed (`metadata_ready`) with no assignment yet, and up to 20 of the workspace's signers; its documents hold up to 2,000 fields between them (a virtual document's being one per signer) and up to 100 copy receivers, documents added later included. Each signer is listed once and is on at least one document; a document can have any of them. Every signer signs at once, with no `step`, so a digital-certificate signer is alone on each of their documents, and signs only virtual ones. A document is signed on its virtual page or, with `method: collect` and its `entries`, on fields placed on its pages, as on an assignment: its signers are the ones on its fields, and they sign it with their envelope link through the document's own signing routes. Each document can take its own `expires_at` and `copy_receiver_ids`, as on an assignment. The envelope is charged as one document, whatever its documents, each signer's notifications and identity check once for the whole envelope, and each digital-certificate signature on every document it is made on; `max_total_credits` caps the total. A refused request creates and charges nothing. Send an `Idempotency-Key` header to retry safely. `POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/estimate-cost` takes the same body and answers what creating it would cost, as an assignment's estimate does, creating and charging nothing.

### Invitations and signing

One invitation goes to each signer for all their documents, named after the envelope and listing the documents they still have to sign and, by e-mail, those they already signed; a send that fails is recorded in that signer's `notification_history` and doesn't undo the envelope. Their link signs or declines their documents of the envelope together (`PUT /v1/signers/documents/sign-multiple`, `PUT /v1/signers/documents/decline-multiple`) and reaches only that envelope's documents: `GET /v1/sign?document_id=` opens any of them the signer is on (and `POST /v1/sign/certified-copy` takes `document_id` in its body), and every route with a document in its path (signing, confirm-data, reject, its reads, downloads and pages) acts on that document, the link's e-mail or WhatsApp verification carried there once. It stays open until the signer is done with every one of them, plus 30 minutes; after that it answers `410`, except `GET /v1/sign` and `GET /v1/signers/{signerId}/document` (the signer's status), `POST /v1/sign/certified-copy`, `GET /v1/sign/theme` and `GET /v1/sign/logo`. `PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/signers/{signerId}/resend` reminds a signer of the whole envelope at once: one message from their first link, charged once, and recorded on each document they still have to sign. A document's own reminder still goes per document, with that document's own link, and carries the envelope's invitation. An identity-check signer (`IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic`) checks once, with any of their links: one check covers every document of the envelope they are on. In review, they view and sign them all, and each waits for the review once signed (`pending_identity_review`). The review is read and decided through any of those documents' identity-verification routes and recorded on each: approving releases each for certification, every certificate printing the check, and rejecting cancels the whole envelope as its cancel does, one notice per person. A check the provider declines locks them out of every document of it, cancelling nothing. A document added for them once approved is verified too. A digital-certificate signer signs each of their documents with their certificate, on its own, one PAdES signature per document: `POST /v1/signers/certificate/start` and `/complete` take the document in `document_id` with their link, and sign-multiple never covers their documents. Each document is certificated on its own, with its own webhooks, which keep their shape, and its own e-mails, titled with the envelope's name and the document's: `GET /v1/documents/{documentId}?expand=envelope_id` says which envelope a document is in, and `?expand=envelope` its id and name.

### Embedded signers

A signer sent with `embedded: true` signs inside your app, as on an assignment, on every document of the envelope, the ones added later too: the plan needs the Embed feature, and the signer Bypass, Email or WhatsApp verification. Their `signing_urls` entry has no link (`url` is `null`). Mint an embed session (`POST /v1/documents/{documentId}/assignments/{assignmentId}/signers/{signerId}/embed-sessions`) on any of their documents still waiting for them: the frame lists every document still in the envelope they have to sign, and the code their envelope invitation carries verifies them there, as does the code a reminder of the envelope or of that document sends.

### Reading and cancelling

`GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes` lists the workspace's envelopes, the most recent first (`search` finds part of a name; `status` is `open` or `closed`), and `GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}` reads one: its documents in order (`position`), each with its status and its signers (name, e-mail, WhatsApp number and whether they signed), and how many are in each status. An envelope has no status of its own. `GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/activities` is its trail: the activities of every document it has had, one taken out included and none deleted, newest first, each naming its document. `GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/download/{artifactName}` zips that file of every document, in order (`bundle`: a folder per document). `GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/documents?envelope_id=` lists an envelope's documents in full. `PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/cancel` cancels every document that can still be cancelled and answers what happened to each; it is safe to repeat. Each document's owner, each signer and each copy receiver is told once for the whole cancel: e-mails are titled with the envelope's name and list the documents cancelled, the owner's also those every signer signed, which stay valid; WhatsApp names the envelope. While any of its documents is open, a document of an envelope, or one taken out of it, can't be deleted on its own (`409` with code `EnvelopeOpen`): cancel the envelope first.

### Changing and deleting

`PATCH /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}` renames an envelope, changes its message or puts its documents in a new order (`document_ids`). Nothing is sent: the reads and every notice from then on follow the change. `POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/documents` adds a document to an open envelope for some of its signers, checked as on creation and charging only its digital-certificate signatures (the envelope paid for its document and its signers' notifications and identity checks), up to 20 documents in all: each of them is sent the envelope's invitation again, with the link of their first invitation, now listing it (`409` with code `EnvelopeClosed` once every document is closed). No one new joins an envelope once it was sent. `DELETE /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}/documents/{documentId}` takes an open document out: it is cancelled, its people are told, and the other documents carry on (`409` with code `DocumentClosed` for a document already closed). The links sent from it keep opening the rest. `DELETE /v1/accounts/{accountId}/envelopes/{envelopeId}` deletes an envelope once every document of it is closed (`409` with code `EnvelopeOpen` before): its documents stay as ordinary documents.

### Deleting the workspace

Deleting the workspace cancels its pending documents, envelopes' included, and blanks each envelope's name and message.


### Contracts

Contract terms tracked on documents: counterparty, value, dates and renewal terms. A contract always belongs to a document of the workspace, and tracking it never changes how that document is uploaded, sent or signed.

### How the flow works

1. **Have the document first.** Upload it with `POST /v1/accounts/{accountId}/documents`, or pick one already in the workspace, and keep its `id`. No call creates a document and its contract terms together.
2. **Set its terms.** `PUT /v1/accounts/{accountId}/documents/{documentId}/contract` with the terms. Any time: right after the upload, while the document is out for signature, or long after it was signed. A contract that ended before it was tracked is registered as it ended (`expired` with a past `end_date`, or `terminated`). A cancelled, declined or expired document takes no new terms. If this call fails, the document stays uploaded and the terms can be sent again.
3. **Record a change with a signed instrument** (optional). Upload the amendment, renewal or termination document, then `PUT` its own `.../contract` with `parent_document_id` (the contract's document), `relation_type` and the terms it changes. The change applies to the contract once that document is signed (at once if it already is), and `document_contract_amended` is recorded.
4. **Let the hourly run keep it current.** Every active contract is walked by the Brasília calendar day: the renewal notice when the notice period starts, warnings 45 and 30 days before the end date, and, the day after it, the next term for an auto-renew contract or `expired` for the others. Each records its `document_contract_*` event and e-mails the contract's owner. The same run hands the contracts of an owner who left the workspace, however they left, to the first owner still an active member.
5. **Or change it directly.** `PUT` edits the terms, `POST .../renew` starts the next term and `POST .../terminate` closes the contract.
6. **Read it.** `GET /v1/accounts/{accountId}/contracts` lists the workspace's contracts; `GET .../documents/{documentId}/contract` reads one with its amendments; `GET /v1/documents/{documentId}` says whether a document has one (`has_contract`). Every change is an event on the document's activities and a webhook.

### Who can write

Contract tracking comes with every standard plan, the free plan too. A write needs it on the workspace's current subscription, and answers `403` (`PlanRestricted`) when the subscription lacks it (a custom contract that leaves it out, or an administrator's removal) or when contract tracking is turned off for the whole service; reads stay open. Any active member of the workspace, owner or organizer, may set terms, link amendments, renew and terminate; an OAuth app needs `documents:write` to write and `documents:read` to read.

### Errors and conflicts

A refused write lists every problem in `errors`, each with its `field` and a stable `code`; the codes and the rules behind them are in the `400` response. A write that sends the `updated_at` it read is refused with `409` if the contract changed meanwhile.

### When a paid plan ends

Terminating a paid plan moves the workspace to the free plan at once, and the free plan tracks contracts too. A paid plan that expires (a payment past due inside the grace period keeps it) leaves the workspace without a current plan until a request looks its plan up, as any contract write does, which moves it to the free plan. Until then the hourly run leaves its contracts as they are and signed amendments wait. The first run after catches up: a contract past its end date moves to the term running that day, on its own renewal cycle, or expires; waiting amendments apply in signing order; alerts whose window passed meanwhile are not sent.

### Verification & Notification Methods

When you create an assignment, each signer can be configured with a **verification method** (how the signer proves their identity before signing) and a **notification method** (how the signer is told a signature is being requested). Exactly one notification method is allowed per signer; `notification_methods` is an array for historical reasons, and sending more than one entry returns `400`. These are set per signer via `signers[].verification_method` and `signers[].notification_methods` on the **Create assignment** endpoint.

Verification and notification are **coupled** — you may send one, both or neither, and the missing side is inferred. If neither is sent, both default to `Email`.

### Verification methods

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Email` | The signer receives a verification code by email that must be entered before signing. |
| `Whatsapp` | The signer receives a verification code over WhatsApp that must be entered before signing. Requires the WhatsApp notification channel — the two always travel together. |
| `DigitalCertificate` | The signer signs with their own ICP-Brasil digital certificate (A1/A3) from their device using the Web PKI browser extension, producing a qualified PAdES signature on the document. **Only on `virtual` assignments**: the certificate flow does not fill placed fields, so it can't be combined with them (`collect`, or a template with placed signer fields). |
| `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic` | Identity document verification. Before seeing the document, the signer consents, photographs an identity document, takes a photo holding it and passes a liveness check; the result must match the CPF and name you registered for the signer. See **Identity document verification** below. |

| Code | Requirements | Cost per signer (verification + its notification) |
|------|--------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `Email` | Signer must have an email address. | 0 credits (the Email notification) |
| `Whatsapp` | Signer must have a `whatsapp_phone_number`; available only on paid subscriptions. | 0.45 credits (the WhatsApp notification, which this method requires) |
| `DigitalCertificate` | Account must have the **Digital Certificate** feature (Standard and Pro plans). Signer must have a CPF in `government_id`. Each digital-certificate signer must be **alone in its signing step**, and the assignment must be `virtual` (no placed fields); a `collect` assignment, or a template with placed signer fields, returns `400`. | 0.5 credits + its notification |
| `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic` | Account must have the **identity document verification** feature, enabled on request. Signer must have a full name and a valid CPF in `government_id` (a CNPJ is refused). | Your plan's verification price (see below) + its notification |

> **How verification is priced.** `Email`, `Whatsapp` and `DigitalCertificate` verification carry no price of their own — you are billed for the **notification** they are paired with (plus, for `DigitalCertificate`, the signature itself). Because verification and notification are coupled, choosing `Whatsapp` verification also chooses the WhatsApp notification, so a WhatsApp-verified signer costs 0.45 credits against 0 credits for an email-verified one. The column above is that combined per-signer cost, which is what the **Estimate assignment cost** endpoint returns.

> **Digital Certificate cost.** Unlike `Email` and `Whatsapp` verification (whose only cost is the notification), the digital-certificate signature itself is charged **0.5 credits per digital-certificate signer**, on top of the notification cost; in an envelope, on every document the signer signs. The charge is applied when the assignment is created, and appears in the **Estimate assignment cost** breakdown under the `SignatureDigitalCertificate` code.

> **Identity document verification cost.** `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic` is charged per signer, on top of the notification cost, at a price that depends on your plan (below); in an envelope, once per signer for the whole envelope. The charge is applied when the assignment is created, and appears in the **Estimate assignment cost** breakdown under the `VerificationIdDocumentFaceMatchBasic` code.

| Plan | Price per signer |
|------|------------------|
| Free | 1.5 credits |
| Standard | 1 credit |
| Pro | 0.5 credits |
| Other plans and enterprise contracts | 0.25 credits |

### Notification methods

The notification method is what delivers the signing invitation to the signer. Each notification has a credit cost charged when the assignment is created (and again when a notification is resent).

| Code | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `Email` | Sends an email invitation with a link to sign the document. |
| `Whatsapp` | Sends a WhatsApp message with a link to sign the document. |

| Code | Requirements | Cost (per signer) |
|------|--------------|-------------------|
| `Email` | Signer must have an email address. | 0 credits |
| `Whatsapp` | Signer must have a `whatsapp_phone_number`; available only on paid subscriptions. | 0.45 credits |

### Coupling rules

Only matching combinations are allowed; an invalid pairing returns `400 Bad Request`.

| Verification method | Allowed notification methods |
|---------------------|------------------------------|
| `Email` | `Email` |
| `Whatsapp` | `Whatsapp` |
| `DigitalCertificate` | `Email` or `Whatsapp` |
| `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic` | `Email` or `Whatsapp` (inferred: `Email`) |

Exactly one notification method is allowed per signer — `notification_methods` takes a single-element array, and a second entry is rejected with `400` before the pairing above is even checked.

### Default behavior (inference)

- **Neither specified** — both default to `Email`.
- **Only `verification_method`** — `notification_methods` is inferred from it (e.g. `Whatsapp` verification → `Whatsapp` notification, and with it that channel's cost).
- **Only `notification_methods`** — `verification_method` is inferred from it.
- **Both specified** — used as-is, subject to the coupling rules above.

### Costs

Notification cost is charged **per signer**, on top of the document cost. For example:

- 2 signers notified by email = 0 credits
- 2 signers notified by WhatsApp = 0.9 credits

Verification follows the same arithmetic, because it is the notification that is billed: 2 signers **verified** by WhatsApp are necessarily notified by WhatsApp, and therefore also cost 0.9 credits. The exceptions are `DigitalCertificate` and `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic`, which add their own per-signer charge on top of the notification.

Use the **Estimate assignment cost** endpoint to preview the exact total (documents + notifications + verification and signature charges) before creating an assignment.

### Notification timing and sequential signing

By default every signer is notified as soon as the assignment is created. When you set `signers[].step` to define a signing order, each signer's notification is held until their step is activated: step 1 is notified at creation, and a later step is notified only after every signer in the previous step has finished.

### Identity document verification

With `IdDocumentFaceMatchBasic`, identity verification is the signer's first step:

1. The signer opens the invitation and gives consent (**Start identity document verification**). The response carries the capture `url`, which the signer opens on their phone to photograph the document, take a photo holding it and pass the liveness check.
2. Back on the signing page, **Identity document verification status** reports the result. The document's signer list also shows it in `identity_verification_status`.

| Result | What happens |
|--------|--------------|
| `Approved` | The document, CPF and name matched. The signer views and signs normally. |
| `InReview` | The service could not decide (for instance, the name differs slightly from the document). The signer **still views and signs**; the account is emailed to review. Once every signer has signed, the document waits in `pending_identity_review` instead of being certificated. |
| `Declined` | The verification failed. The signer cannot sign this document. |
| `Expired` | The capture link lapsed before anything was submitted; the signer may start again. |
| `Abandoned` | The signer left the capture unfinished. As with `Declined`, they cannot restart; send a new document to verify them again. |

**Reviewing.** A user of the account opens the review with **Signer identity review** (reasons, expected vs. read data, checks and evidence images, each fetched with **Signer identity review image** while the review is open), then decides with **Decide signer identity review**:

- **Approved** — the document is certificated once every signer has signed and no other review is pending.
- **Rejected** — the document is cancelled (`rejected_by_user`, with the reviewer as the user) and every signer receives the usual cancellation notice. The reviewer's note is never shown to signers.

An unreviewed document still expires at its deadline, and deleting a `pending_identity_review` document cancels it and notifies the signers. A signer under review in a sequential flow completes their step, so the next step is notified right away.

Each step of the process is recorded as a `signer_identity_*` activity and webhook event (see the **Event catalog**). A verification belongs to one document and is never reused for another; in an envelope, one check covers every document of it the signer is on (see **Envelopes**).


### Assignments

Request signatures on a document and estimate their cost.

### Signing

Signer-facing endpoints: view, sign and decline documents using a signer access code. An access code stops opening the document 30 minutes after its signer is done (signed, or the document was declined, cancelled, expired or failed); the code of a document of an envelope, 30 minutes after the signer is done with every document of the envelope they are on, and it opens, signs and declines only documents of that envelope (documents outside it answer `404`, and `400` in sign-multiple and decline-multiple): from then on `GET /v1/sign` and `GET /v1/signers/{signerId}/document` return only the signer's status, `POST /v1/sign/certified-copy` sends the certified copy again, `GET /v1/sign/theme` and `GET /v1/sign/logo` still brand the page, and every other endpoint answers `410`. The certified copy is never downloaded with an access code; it is sent to the signer by e-mail or WhatsApp.

### Templates

Reusable document templates, their roles, fields and tags.

### Fields

Reusable field definitions used on templates and assignments.

### Tags

Workspace-scoped labels attachable to documents and templates.

### OAuth

The token, revocation and userinfo endpoints an OAuth application calls, and this API's protected-resource metadata. New to OAuth with Assinafy? Read **OAuth Integration Guide** first. The authorization server's own metadata is served at `https://auth.assinafy.com.br/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`, not on this API: read endpoint URLs from it instead of hardcoding them.

### Webhooks

Outbound webhook endpoints and delivery history.

An account can register **1 webhook endpoint**, or **up to 3** on paid plans. Each endpoint has its own URL, event list and signing setting, and every active endpoint subscribed to an event receives it. Manage them with the **webhook endpoint** operations; the older `/webhooks/subscriptions` operations still work and act on the account's oldest endpoint.

### Webhook Payloads

This section documents the HTTP request your endpoint receives whenever a subscribed event is triggered, and the shape of the JSON body sent for each event type.

### Delivery contract

When an event occurs, we send an HTTP `POST` request to every active webhook endpoint subscribed to that event. Each endpoint is delivered to independently: a slow or failing endpoint does not delay the others, and each has its own failure count.

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Method | `POST` |
| Content-Type | `application/json` |
| Connection header | `close` |
| `webhook-id` header | Message ID, identical on every attempt of the same event to the same endpoint. Use it to deduplicate. |
| `webhook-timestamp` header | Unix timestamp (seconds) of the attempt. |
| `webhook-signature` header | Only when signing is enabled on the endpoint. See **Verifying signatures**. |
| Success criteria | Any `2xx` response |
| `User-Agent` header | `Assinafy-Webhooks/1.0` |
| Attempts | Up to 6 per event, about 10 minutes apart. A connection error, a timeout, a `408`, a `429` or a `5xx` is retried; any other status is final. |
| Pause | After 10 failed deliveries in a row the endpoint is paused (`is_held` on the endpoint): nothing is sent to it, and we probe it with the oldest event it missed after 3 minutes, then 15, then 60, then every 6 hours. The probe that gets through lifts the pause and the events it missed are delivered oldest first. Editing the endpoint's URL, or sending `is_active: true`, lifts the pause too. |
| Retry endpoint | **Retry webhook delivery** sends one delivery now, even while the endpoint is paused; a delivery that gets through lifts the pause. |
| Response capture | We store the first 2000 characters of your response body for debugging (see **List webhook deliveries**). Delivery entries are kept for 7 days. |

Your endpoint must respond within a reasonable time and return a `2xx` status. Non-`2xx` responses, connection errors and timeouts are all failed deliveries and count toward the pause; each delivery entry says whether another attempt follows (`will_retry`).

### Verifying signatures

Enable signing on an endpoint (`signing_enabled: true`) and every delivery carries a signature that proves it came from us and was not altered or replayed. Signatures follow the [Standard Webhooks](https://www.standardwebhooks.com) specification, so any Standard Webhooks library can verify them; the secret is returned once, as `secret`, in the **Create webhook endpoint** response, and can be read again with **Get webhook endpoint signing secret**. OAuth applications cannot call that endpoint: store the secret from the create response, and if it is lost, get a new one with **Rotate webhook endpoint signing secret**. Turning signing on with **Update webhook endpoint** also returns the new secret once.

To verify by hand:

1. Take the **raw** request body, exactly as received (do not re-serialize the parsed JSON).
2. Build the signed content `{webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{body}`.
3. Base64-decode the part of the secret after the `whsec_` prefix and compute the HMAC-SHA256 of the signed content with it. Base64-encode the result.
4. `webhook-signature` holds one or more space-separated `v1,<signature>` entries; accept the request if any of them equals your value (use a constant-time comparison).
5. Reject requests whose `webhook-timestamp` is more than a few minutes away from your clock, to prevent replays.

```php
$secret = base64_decode(substr($endpointSecret, strlen('whsec_')));
$signedContent = $headers['webhook-id'] . '.' . $headers['webhook-timestamp'] . '.' . $rawBody;
$expected = 'v1,' . base64_encode(hash_hmac('sha256', $signedContent, $secret, true));

$valid = false;
foreach (explode(' ', $headers['webhook-signature']) as $signature) {
    $valid = $valid || hash_equals($expected, $signature);
}
$fresh = abs(time() - (int) $headers['webhook-timestamp']) <= 300;
```

Rotating the secret (**Rotate webhook endpoint signing secret**) takes effect immediately: deliveries sent after the rotation are signed only with the new secret. Rotate with `keep_previous: true` to keep the old one signing for 24 hours: during that time `webhook-signature` carries one signature per secret, space-separated, so a receiver that accepts any matching entry (step 4) keeps verifying while it switches to the new secret. Only the secret just replaced is kept: rotating again within those 24 hours stops the one kept before.

### Common envelope

Every webhook body shares the same top-level structure:

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | integer | Internal activity ID that produced this event. To deduplicate retries, prefer the `webhook-id` header, which also tells deliveries of the same event to different endpoints apart. |
| `event` | string | Event type identifier. See the catalog below and the **List webhook event types** endpoint. |
| `message` | string \\| null | Human-readable message describing the event. May contain token placeholders. Can be `null`. |
| `payload` | object \\| null | Event-specific parameters. Keys vary per event — see the catalog. Can be `null`. |
| `origin` | object \\| null | Where the action was triggered from, when available: `{ ip, user-agent }`. |
| `created_at` | integer | Unix timestamp (seconds) when the event was recorded. |
| `subject` | object | The entity that performed the action. Polymorphic — see below. |
| `object` | object | The entity the action was performed on. Polymorphic — see below. |
| `account_id` | string | The ID of the account that owns this event. Always present. |

### About `subject` and `object`

Both are **polymorphic**: their shape depends on which entity they represent. We always add a `type` property with the entity class name, one of `User`, `Signer`, `Account`, `Document`, or `Template`, or `ActivityEventSubscription` (a webhook endpoint) in a `webhook_test` delivery. The remaining properties match the same fields the REST API returns for that resource. The `object` is serialized with its extra relationships expanded (e.g. a `Document` includes `assignment` and `pages`); the `subject` carries its base fields only. An `object` deleted before the delivery is sent still arrives with its fields as they were when it was deleted (a document cancelled by deleting it has status `rejected_by_user`), and the relationships deleted with it come back empty (`assignment: null`, `pages: []`); a `subject` deleted before the delivery carries only its `type`. Whenever `subject` or `object` is an `Account`, the `integration` property (which includes dispatch history) is removed before sending.

For `document_ready`, `document_processing_failed` and `template_processing_failed`, the `subject` is the `Account` itself — these events are emitted by the system when processing finishes, not by a particular user.

### Event catalog

Each event also has its own entry under **Webhooks** with a complete example body.

| Event | Subject | Object | `payload` keys | Description |
|-------|---------|--------|----------------|-------------|
| `document_uploaded` | User | Document | — | The user uploaded a new document. |
| `document_metadata_ready` | User | Document | — | The document was normalized to PDF and its pages are available. |
| `document_prepared` | User | Document | — | The user prepared a document (fields assigned to signers). |
| `assignment_created` | User | Document | `user_name`, `user_email`, `user_telephone` | The user created an assignment for the document. Includes a snapshot of the creator profile. |
| `document_ready` | Account | Document | — | The document was certificated after every signer signed (and, when a signer's identity was under review, after the account approved it). |
| `document_processing_failed` | Account | Document | `error_message` | The document could not be processed. |
| `signature_requested` | User | Document | `signer_full_name`, `signer_email`, `signer_whatsapp_phone_number`, `notification_method` (`email`, `whatsapp` or `bypass`) | A signer was invited to sign the document: when the assignment is created, or for a later signing step when that step opens, and again for each reminder sent with `PUT /v1/documents/{documentId}/assignments/{assignmentId}/signers/{signerId}/resend`. One event per notification method that went out, named in `notification_method`; with `bypass` nothing is sent, the event marks the signing link as issued, and no reminder goes out by `bypass` (a signer notified only by Bypass is refused). The automatic notice before the deadline, the notice of a new deadline and a send the provider refuses don't send it; a message accepted and later bounced still did. |
| `signer_created` | User | Signer | `signer_full_name` | The user created a new signer. |
| `signer_email_verified` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `signer_email` | The signer's email was verified through a code linked to the document. |
| `signer_whatsapp_verified` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `signer_whatsapp_phone_number` | The signer's WhatsApp number was verified through a code linked to the document. |
| `signer_data_confirmed` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `signer_email`, `signer_whatsapp_phone_number`, `verification_method` | The signer confirmed their data before signing. |
| `signer_viewed_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer opened the document for the first time. |
| `signer_identity_verified` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `evidence` (when available) | The signer passed identity-document verification, directly or after the account's review. |
| `signer_identity_verification_failed` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `reason` | The identity-document verification ended without approval. |
| `signer_identity_review_required` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `reason_codes` | The verification awaits the account's review. The signer can still sign; the document is certificated only after the account approves (status `pending_identity_review` once every signer has signed). |
| `signer_identity_review_approved` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `reviewer_id`, `reviewer_name`, `reason_codes` | A user of the account approved the signer's identity after review. |
| `signer_identity_review_rejected` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name`, `reviewer_id`, `reviewer_name`, `note` | A user of the account rejected the signer's identity after review. The document is cancelled; `user_rejected_document` follows. |
| `signer_signed_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer signed the document. |
| `signer_rejected_document` | Signer | Document | `signer_full_name` | The signer refused to sign the document. |
| `user_rejected_document` | User | Document | `user_name` | The document was cancelled by a user of the account. |
| `template_created` | User | Template | — | The user created a new template. |
| `template_processed` | User | Template | — | A template's metadata was processed and is ready for use. |
| `template_processing_failed` | Account | Template | `error_message` | A template could not be processed. |

`assignment_created` and `document_metadata_ready` have no guaranteed ordering: under the virtual pre-metadata flow, `assignment_created` may fire before `document_metadata_ready`. Treat any unknown field as a forward-compatible addition.

### Embedded Signing

Let your own application show the signing page inside an iframe. An account lists the origins allowed to embed it, then mints a short-lived embed session for each embedded signer. Requires the `Embed` feature; without it the endpoints answer `403` with code `PlanRestricted`.
